title: Chapter 44 – Funeral on the Hill
html:
[Lin Clan – Su Qinghe]

Su Qinghe washes the dead because someone must, and because for twenty years she has been the one who does not flinch.

The hall of ancestors is cold at dawn. It smells of cedar and wet stone and the long sweet rot of lilies, brought from the lower gardens by women who did not know what else to bring. Five bodies lie on five boards, side by side, under white cloth. She has finished four. Her hands are red to the wrist from the basin, and the water is the color of weak tea.

Lin Mao is the fifth.

She folds back the cloth. He is lying as Wenshi laid him, with his hands crossed on his chest and his steel-gray beard combed straight, and his face is calm. They have taken off the cuirass. Under it the shirt is stiff and black from the ribs down. She cuts it away with scissors, carefully, thread by thread, and lays it in the burning basket.

The wound is clean. Two hooks, through the thigh and through the side. She has seen worse. She has dressed worse, in the years before the clan, when she was a river-girl with a bucket of herbs and no name, and men came off the boats with their bellies open. But she has never washed a man she had known for twenty years, who once carried her son through a snowstorm on his back, and who said the same thing every New Year to every child who came to the guardhouse: Count your steps, and you will always know where you are.

She wrings the cloth. She begins at the face.

* * *

"You should let the women do it."

The voice is dry and level and comes from the door. She does not turn.

"The women are with Mao's daughter. And the other four have families who are sleeping." She wipes a thumb across the dead man's brow. "Someone should be here who is not weeping, Wenyuan. It is easier for them."

The Patriarch comes in. He has not slept. His gray robe is creased, and there is ash on his sleeve, and the skin under his eyes is the color of a bruise. He stops at the foot of the board and looks down for a long time.

"I wrote to the Arbiter last night," he says. "Eight pages. Two copies. One by hawk, one by Wenshi's rider. I told them everything but the pangolin."

"And?"

"And the hawk will take four days, and the Arbiter's office is in the habit of reading a petition three weeks after it arrives." His mouth twists. "I do not expect help. I only wanted it written."

"Yes." She lifts Mao's hand, and washes it, finger by finger. "Is it true that Elder Zhong has called the council?"

"At noon."

"To do what?"

"To say what everybody is thinking." Wenyuan rubs his eyes. "That we have a refiner the Blood Shadow wants, a seamwalker they want more, and a nineteen-year-old who throws needles. That four of our men are dead because we would not give up one drunk. That the next wave will be larger." He lets his hand fall. "And that perhaps it was a mistake not to put the old man in a cart, and drive him to the cairn."

Qinghe says nothing. The cloth drips into the basin.

"I do not think he is wrong to say it," says Wenyuan quietly. "I think it is a fair question. I think I should like to be able to answer it better than I can."

* * *

The council meets in the east hall, which is warmer, and which has a long table of black wood where eight generations of Lin patriarchs have signed away or defended the clan's small fortunes.

There are twenty-three at the table. Qinghe sits at its foot, as the clan's only non-blood elder, between Wenqing's empty chair and the old schoolmaster. Wenyuan sits at the head. At his right hand is his brother Wenshi, with his wrist splinted in white wood and his face the color of dough. At the left, Elder Aunt Wenjun, the accountant, stiff and spare in her gray, with her ledger open under her hand.

And across the table, a little apart, with a cup of tea going cold in front of him, is Elder Lin Zhong.

He is seventy-one. He is a broad, heavy, soft-faced man with a white mustache and a voice like warm syrup, and in forty years of council he has never said an unkind word to anyone's face. He is also the largest single holder of the clan's three western farms, and every farmer on those farms is his cousin, his tenant, or his creditor.

"I will say it plainly," says Zhong, "because nobody else will, and because we are among family. Mao is dead. Four are dead. A hundred and forty stones of loot is a poor trade for five lives." He folds his hands on his stomach. "I do not blame the Patriarch. His grief is mine. But a house cannot grieve itself into the ground."

"You have a proposal," Wenyuan says.

"I have a question." Zhong's mild eyes travel along the table. "What is the old refiner to us? A guest. A gifted guest, a kind man, who has done a great deal for our wall and for our ledgers. But he is a guest. The Blood Shadow wants him. We do not know why. We know that they will come again, and that the next time they will not send a single drummer." He spreads his hands. "I propose that we ask him, as a courtesy, whether he would prefer to leave us. With an escort. To a neutral city. With our blessing and our gold."

"He has said he will stay," says Qinghe.

"Has he?" Zhong turns his face to her, kindly. "He is a man who tried to leave a month ago, Madam Su, in the night, with a book under his arm. I would not call that a vow."

It is true. She feels it land on the table like a stone.

"He tried," says Wenshi. His voice is rough and hard. "And my nephew brought him back. And three days later Mao died holding a road for him. I'll not tell a man he's a guest after that."

"Not a guest, then. A debt." Zhong sighs. "Mao's debt, Wenshi. Not yours."

"Mao would not have wanted—"

"Mao is dead, Wenshi." For the first time the syrup in the voice thins, and something hard shows. "He is dead, and his daughter will be a widow's daughter, and tonight the Narrows will be full of wolves. I will not sit here and be told what a dead man would have wanted."

A silence falls. Nobody speaks. The old schoolmaster coughs into his hand.

Then, at Qinghe's elbow, a chair scrapes.

* * *

Wenqing has come in late.

He is standing in the doorway in his old green herbalist's gown, with his hair uncombed and his hands hanging by his sides. His face is gray. His eyes have the empty, scoured look of a man who has been awake three days and has not been told it is allowed to stop. In his belt is a short curved knife with a green-gray blade, wiped clean.

"I killed her," says Wenqing.

Nobody breathes.

"The woman. The sister. Mei Lian. I was on the rope, and I let go, and I put the knife in her back, and I felt it go through." He says it as if reading a prescription. "She said, you are pruning me. I said I was sorry. I was." He swallows. "I have been apologizing to her since the hour it happened. I have said it over four hundred times, I think. I have not stopped."

"Wenqing," Wenyuan says softly. "Sit down."

"No. Please. I would like to say it." He looks at Zhong. The mild, ruined eyes are quite steady. "Elder, I am an herbalist. I have tended this clan's children for twenty-two years. I have set bones and delivered babies and sat up three nights with a boy who had the red fever. I have never raised my hand to anyone in anger in my life." He wets his lips. "Three days ago I killed a woman because she was about to kill my nephew. I would do it again tomorrow. I want it understood that I would do it again tomorrow, and that if you hand Lin Hu to the Blood Shadow in a cart, I will not be able to look at the face of anyone who agrees."

Zhong sits very still.

"That's not an argument," he says at last, gently.

"No," says Wenqing. "It isn't. I haven't got one. I only know I will not give a man to them whom I have fed."

He sits down. His shoulders are shaking. Qinghe puts a hand on his arm, and he does not seem to notice.

"This is an emotional matter," says Zhong, to the table. "I understand it. But the question stands."

"It does," says Wenyuan.

He has not moved. His eyes are on the black wood of the table. When he lifts them, they are very calm.

"Let me answer it, then," he says. "Zhong, you are right that I do not know why the Sect wants Hu. I believe it is for what he carries in his head, and I believe the thing they want it for is not a thing the clan will survive having done. But I do not know. Nor do you." He folds his hands. "What I know is that four men are dead on the Salt Road, and the Sect did not ask for a refiner when it sent them. It sent a drummer. Mu sent a drummer to kill a clan. The refiner was an excuse. If you give him the old man, he will send them anyway, with a different excuse, in a different month."

"You cannot know that."

"I cannot. But I have known men like Mu all my life." Wenyuan's voice is low, almost gentle. "They do not take what you give them. They take what they were already taking, and thank you for the rope."

A long pause. Zhong shakes his heavy head.

"I would like a vote," he says.

"You shall have one." Wenyuan looks round the table. "I ask it as a Patriarch and I will abide by it. But I ask something first." He turns, at last, to the woman at the foot of the table. "Qinghe. Will you tell them what you told me last night?"

She had not expected it. She sets down her cup.

* * *

She stands, because it is easier to speak standing.

"I am not a Lin," she says. "I came to this hill with nothing, and the clan was good to me, and I have tried to repay it. I have no talent for council. I will say two things and sit down."

The room waits.

"First. In four weeks, this clan has killed seven of the Blood Shadow. Seven. Two scouts in the forest. A rogue called Ke Tian and his man, in the rafters of our granary. A drummer, a sister. And not one of those deaths was done by an ordinary guard in an ordinary fight. They were done by preparation. By a prepared road, a prepared rafter, a prepared wire. By people who knew where to stand." She lets that settle. "Mu does not know who is doing it. I think that frightens him. A man who has spent sixty years being the most frightening thing in any room is not accustomed to being afraid."

"And the second?" says Zhong.

"The second is that I will not tell you who is doing it." She meets his eyes. "I will tell you only that it is someone you would not guess, and that if you vote to put any one of us in a cart, you will be putting that person into the cart too."

She sits.

It is a lie, in part. She is not sure, even now, how much of it is a lie. She has been sitting on the second half of that sentence since two nights ago, when she washed the blood off a nineteen-year-old's ribs in the light of a single candle, and found his body had been doing what it was never meant to do.

* * *

The vote is eleven to eight, with four who do not raise a hand.

Zhong takes it well. He rises, bows to the Patriarch, and kisses Elder Aunt Wenjun's wrist in the old courtly way. At the door he stops, and says, in his warm slow voice, to nobody in particular: "I hope I am wrong. I have never hoped it so hard."

Then he is gone. And Qinghe, who has stood in this hall for twenty years, finds that her knees are trembling.

"Well done," says Wenjun quietly, at her shoulder.

"I did nothing."

"You frightened them." The old woman is turning pages in her ledger, and does not look up. "That is what the Patriarch wanted. He could not do it. He is too honest." She makes a small dry sound. "I counted. Five of those eleven would have voted the other way if you had not spoken. I wish to know, Qinghe, whether you are very much cleverer than you look."

"No."

"Mm," says Wenjun. She shuts the ledger. "Then somebody is."

* * *

Two nights ago, after the Narrows, she binds his rib by candlelight.

He sits on the edge of the bed with his shirt off, very straight, and lets her. The bruise is already the size of her palm, a spreading purple-black stain over the left side of his chest. The rib under it is cracked clean through. She feels it with two fingers and he does not make a sound.

"It will knit in a month," she says. "If you do not do anything stupid."

"Yes, Mother."

She winds the linen tight. Her hands work, and her eyes, against her will, do what they have trained to do for twenty years, and read. The calluses on his fingertips, thin and even, in a ring around each nail. The faint white scars across the heel of his right hand, where a thread has bitten. The shoulders, narrow and hard as a young bird's. And under the skin, when she lays her palm flat over his heart, a faint steady heat, too steady for a youth of nineteen. It is the heat of a body that has been taught to run on very little for very long.

Seventh stage, she thinks. It is a number she has never said aloud. The Register thinks he is second. Wenyuan thinks he is third, and is afraid to ask. She has known for months, in the way a mother knows what is under her child's quilt, and has chosen not to look, because looking would mean asking how.

"Who taught you to throw a needle like that?" she says.

"Nobody." His eyes are on the candle. "I watched the lamp. Hu showed me how a thread holds a bead. I practiced."

"On what?"

"A straw target. And then a rat."

She stops winding. "A rat."

"It was in the granary. It was eating Hu's grain." He is quite serious. "I wanted to know how the needle felt. When it went into something that was alive."

The linen is very white in the candlelight. Something small stirs in the folds of the quilt, a pale scaled head, and looks at her with one black bead of an eye.

"And how did it feel?" she asks, when she can.

"Like a lie," says Jian. "Like I had been told it would be hard, and it wasn't." He looks up, at last, and his face is quite calm, and quite old. "That is the part I do not like, Mother. That it isn't."

She ties the knot. She sits there, on the edge of her son's bed, with her hand on his shoulder, for a very long time, and does not say anything at all.

* * *

They burn the dead on the hillside at dusk.

It is a Lin custom. Five pyres of cedar and pine, built on the bare shoulder of the ridge above the ancestral hall, so that the smoke goes straight up into the sky and the ancestors can see who is coming. The whole clan is there. Four hundred people, in white. The women keen, a thin high wavering sound like geese. The men stand with their heads bowed. Children are hushed with a hand on a shoulder.

Qinghe stands among them. She has washed, and put on a white robe, and tied her hair up with a strip of undyed cotton. Her hands are quite steady. Wenshi is on her left, gaunt, with his splinted wrist. Jian is on her right.

He has not spoken since noon.

He is wearing the gray funeral robe, a size too large, with the sleeves rolled to the wrist. He stands very straight, with his hands at his sides and his face turned toward the pyres, and the firelight makes a mask of it. Something small and pale peeps out of his collar. She does not remark on it. She has long since stopped.

The captain's daughter lights the fifth pyre. She is a thin girl of nineteen with her baby on her hip. She stands with the torch at arm's length and looks at it for a long moment, and then she steps forward and puts it to the cedar, and the flame goes up with a soft soft roar.

Nobody makes a sound.

Count your steps, thinks Qinghe, and you will always know where you are.

* * *

It is later, past midnight, when she goes to his room.

She has been putting it off. She has found things to do. She has seen Wenqing to his bed with a cup of poppy and white willow, and sat with Mao's daughter an hour, and looked in on Wenshi and on Hu, who was sitting in the dark in the granary with his bent iron rod across his knees, and who looked up at her with such stricken, enormous gratitude that she could not bear it, and left.

Now she stands in the passage outside her son's door, in her slippers, with a candle, and listens.

Nothing. Not the creak of a floorboard. Not a breath. She tries the handle, and it gives.

The room is empty.

The bed is made. The quilt is tucked. On the desk, a lamp burns low beside a stack of Hu's drawing paper, and on top of the paper lies a single sheet in Jian's small neat hand. She picks it up.

It is a map.

It is a very simple map, in black ink, of the quarry on the northern slope. A square for the shed, a circle for the spoil heaps, a wavy line for the stream. At the eastern edge, where the stone has been cut away in great steps, a cross. And beside the cross, in a tiny script, three words.

Blood. Fresh. Dragging.

She stands there with the candle shaking in her hand.

Mei Ru. The sister who escaped in the mist. The one who looked at him with her hand on her mouth and said you will pay for that. She had a wound, a blood-link torn out of her arm. She cannot have gone far. A hurt Drip, cut from her twin, would go to ground in the nearest dark place, where she could lie and bleed and think.

And he has been counting how far.

Qinghe sets down the paper. She sets down the candle. She presses both hands flat against the desk.

I taught him to move in the Veil. I taught him not to be seen. I taught him it was a thing a mother teaches a son who must live among wolves. The thought is cold and exact, and she turns it round, and round, looking for the place where it is wrong. I did not teach him to hunt.

Who did?

On the shelf above the desk, where Hu's old pencil case used to stand, there is a small round pebble, polished smooth. She picks it up. It is warm. In its pale surface she sees her own face, long and drawn, with the candle in it, very small.

She puts it down.

He is nineteen years old, she says to herself, slowly, in the dark. He is nineteen, and he has killed more men than most of the Guard.

Then, with a calm she does not feel, she takes a cloak from the hook behind the door, and a short thin knife from her sleeve, and goes out into the night.

* * *

She does not run. She walks, quick and quiet, with her hood up and the Veil settled over her like water. It is the one gift she has that she is sure of. The slope is black and frost-cold. A thin wind is picking at the pines. Behind her, on the ridge, the last of the pyres is a dull red eye, and the smell of cedar smoke is in her hair.

At the edge of the quarry she stops.

She can see him. She does not know how. The moon is a pale curved blade low in the east, and in its light the quarry is a great gray bowl, its steps laid out like the seats of an old theater. In the middle of it, small and dark and perfectly still, a figure stands with its back to her.

A boy, in a gray funeral robe too long for him.

He is not looking at the cross on his own map. He is looking at the foot of the east wall, where a heap of broken stone lies in shadow, and where, at its base, something is moving. It moves a little. It stops. It moves again.

A long dark trail runs from it across the gravel to a place where the stone has been smeared with red.

Qinghe's mouth goes dry.

Pebble, she thinks. She does not know why. It is the name the boy gave it. Pebble knows where she is. He has not gone out to look. He has gone out to finish.

She takes one step.

And then, so softly that she is not sure she hears it, the boy says, without turning his head: "Mother, I know you are there. Please do not come closer. She is not alone."

Qinghe stops.

"Please," says Jian again, very quietly. "I can explain. I will. But not yet." The small dark figure raises one hand, and in the moonlight she sees the glint of a thin gray needle, and the thread of Qi that runs from it to the stone, fine as spider-silk. "I need you to be very quiet. And I need you to look at the heap of stone behind her."

She looks.

It is not a heap of stone. It is a fold in the earth, a long dark seam in the slope, no wider than a hand, hanging in the air above the gravel like a tear in cloth. Light is seeping out of it. A pale, green, living light, the color of new leaves in spring.

And through it, very faintly, comes a smell she has not smelled in twenty years, since the river, since the boats, since the last time she was a girl with a bucket of herbs.

It is the smell of the wet black earth of an old, old garden.

"What," she whispers, "is that?"

"I don't know yet," says Jian. "But Pebble does. And I think Mei Ru found it first."
